t: Find Right Interval — Binary Search on Starts
o: For each interval we must find the interval whose start is the smallest value that is at least the current interval's end. Since starts are unique, this is a classic 'smallest element >= target' query. In Example 2, for end=3 of [2,3] the smallest start >= 3 is 3 (interval [3,4], index 0), and for end=2 of [1,2] it's start 2 (index 1). With n up to 2*10^4, an O(n^2) brute force (~4*10^8 comparisons) is borderline but a binary search over sorted starts gives O(n log n), which is comfortably fast.
k: The problem reduces to: for each end, find the minimum start >= end — a successor query solvable by binary search.
Starts are unique, so sorting pairs of (start, original index) lets us map a found start back to its interval index.
If even the largest start is smaller than some end, no right interval exists; answer -1.

a.i: For every interval i, scan all intervals j and track the one with the smallest start_j satisfying start_j >= end_i. This directly mirrors the definition and needs no preprocessing. It works because starts are unique so ties never occur, but its quadratic cost is wasteful given the sorted structure available.
s: For each i, initialize best = -1 and bestStart = infinity.
Loop over all j; if start_j >= end_i and start_j < bestStart, update bestStart and best = j.
Store best in the answer array and return it.
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n intervals we scan all n candidates.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the output array.

a.i: Sort the (start, index) pairs by start once. Then each query 'smallest start >= end_i' becomes a standard lower-bound binary search on the sorted starts. Because starts are unique, the matched start uniquely identifies the original interval via its stored index. Sorting costs O(n log n) once, and each of the n queries costs O(log n).
s: Build an array of pairs (start_i, i) and sort it by start.
Extract the sorted starts into a separate array for binary searching.
For each interval i, binary search for the leftmost position where start >= end_i.
If such a position exists, answer with the stored original index; otherwise answer -1.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; each of the n queries is O(log n).
a.sp: O(n) — for the sorted pairs, starts array, and output.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly to show you understand the problem, then go straight to sort + binary search as the expected solution. Key pitfalls: forgetting to keep original indices when sorting (starts are unique, so pairing start with index is safe); using upper_bound instead of lower_bound (we need start >= end, inclusive); and handling the case where no start qualifies (return -1). Edge cases include a single interval (always -1 unless it can be its own right interval, e.g. [1,1]), negative coordinates (binary search handles them naturally), and points where start == end allowing self-match. Likely follow-ups: what if starts were not unique (then tie-break by index or report any/minimum index), or streaming queries against a fixed set of intervals (precompute sorted starts once, answer each query in O(log n)).
